title: Rallies Across the US Encourage People to Vote Early
summary:
On Saturday, people gathered in cities and towns across the United States for rallies urging voters to cast their ballots early in the midterm elections. Midterm elections happen halfway through a president's four-year term. This year, Election Day is November 3.

The rallies were organized by the No Kings network, a group opposed to President Donald Trump. Organizers described the hundreds of events as nonpartisan, meaning not tied to one political party. However, the rallies built on nearly two years of No Kings marches by people unhappy with Trump's presidency.

In Washington, D.C., a band played for what appeared to be a few hundred people near the Lincoln Memorial. Even though the weather was chilly, many people in caps and coats danced. Signs in the crowd said "VOTE EARLY" and "HANDS OFF MY VOTE!" Rallies also took place in New York City and Atlanta.

In Atlanta, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond asked the crowd to encourage others to vote. He compared voting to a superpower. "You don't see Superman giving up his power," he said. "Be a super hero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote."

Voting by mail has become a topic of disagreement. Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting and has claimed, without evidence, that fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election. On Thursday, his administration sued election officials in California. It asked a judge to stop the state from counting mail-in ballots from people the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.

The same day, three Democratic senators wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche. They asked the Justice Department to promise not to seize ballots or other election materials before the midterm results are certified.
why_it_matters: The rallies and the lawsuit show how Americans are debating how voting should work, which shapes who chooses the country's leaders.
